# Benjamin Graham: The Intelligent Investor (Revised Edition, with Jason Zweig Commentary)

Source: [intelligent.md](../../../../../intelligent.md)

## 1. Core Philosophy

- **Investment vs speculation (Ch. 1):** "An investment operation is one which, upon thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return. Operations not meeting these requirements are speculative."
- Speculation isn't forbidden, but keep it in a separate, small account. Zweig: cap "mad money" at **10%** of assets and never mix it with investment accounts.
- **Two investor types:**
  - *Defensive (passive):* wants safety and freedom from effort. Today: low-cost total-market index fund, or the strict Ch. 14 screen.
  - *Enterprising (active):* will put in time and skill for better-than-average results. Needs real analysis; half-hearted effort does worse than passive.
- Returns depend on the intelligent effort you apply, not on how much risk you take.
- **Inflation (Ch. 2):** stocks protect against inflation only partly and unreliably. Bonds alone are not safe either. That's why the portfolio holds both. Zweig: TIPS (in tax-deferred accounts) and REITs as inflation hedges.
- **Market level (Ch. 3):** compare earnings yield and dividend yield with bond yields. Zweig: use the Shiller ratio (price ÷ 10-yr inflation-adjusted avg earnings). Above ~20 has historically led to poor future returns; below ~10 to strong ones.

## 2. Mr. Market & Market Fluctuations (Ch. 8)

- Mr. Market is your manic-depressive business partner who quotes a price every day. Accept his offer when it suits you, ignore it otherwise. His mood is not information about value.
- The investor's main problem, and worst enemy, is likely to be himself.
- A true investor is never forced to sell and can treat quotes as optional. Price declines are a real loss only if you must sell or the business itself deteriorates.
- Don't try to time the market with forecasts. Formula timing (e.g., Dow theory) stopped working once it became popular.
- Conservative investors should concentrate on stocks selling **no more than ~1/3 above tangible asset value**. That links price to a solid base and makes declines less frightening.
- Growth stocks at high multiples fall harder (IBM −50% in 1961–62; Xerox, Texas Instruments −80% when expectations broke).
- Zweig: dot-com examples (Inktomi to $0.25 from $231; CMGI +940% then −99%). Losses hurt about 2× as much as equal gains please. People buy more when prices rise and less when they fall, which is backwards.

## 3. Asset Allocation (Ch. 4)

- Stocks between **25% and 75%**, bonds the rest. Default **50/50**.
- Shift toward 25% stocks when prices look dangerously high; toward 75% only when stocks are clearly cheap (e.g., after a severe bear market). This is valuation-based, not a forecast.
- Rebalance when the mix drifts ~5 points (e.g., at 55% stocks, sell 1/11 of stocks). Zweig: rebalance on a fixed schedule (every 6 months, or yearly).
- Bonds: high-grade only for defensive investors. Choose taxable vs tax-exempt munis based on tax bracket. Zweig: use low-cost bond funds (building your own diversified bond portfolio needs ~$100,000+).
- Zweig: 100% stocks only if you have steady income, a long horizon, proven calm in bear markets, and an emergency reserve.

## 4. Defensive Investor Common-Stock Rules (Ch. 5)

1. Diversify adequately but not excessively: **10–30 issues**.
2. Large, prominent, conservatively financed companies (common equity ≥ half of total capitalization).
3. Long record of continuous dividends (Graham: since 1950, i.e., ~20 yrs; Zweig: at least 10).
4. Price limit: **≤ 25× average earnings of past 7 years and ≤ 20× trailing 12-month earnings**. This rules out almost all popular growth stocks.

- Dollar-cost averaging works: fixed sums at regular intervals buy more shares when prices are low.
- Defensive investors shouldn't own growth stocks at high multiples; there's too much speculative content in the price.

## 5. Defensive Stock Screen: Seven Criteria (Ch. 14) [verified]

| # | Criterion | Threshold |
|---|-----------|-----------|
| 1 | Adequate size | ≥ $100M annual sales (industrial); ≥ $50M total assets (utility). 1972 dollars; scale up heavily for today (Zweig suggests very large caps or index funds). |
| 2 | Strong financial condition | Current ratio ≥ **2:1**; long-term debt ≤ net current assets (working capital). Utilities: debt ≤ 2× equity at book. |
| 3 | Earnings stability | Positive earnings each of past **10 years** |
| 4 | Dividend record | Uninterrupted for at least **20 years** |
| 5 | Earnings growth | ≥ **1/3** increase in per-share earnings over 10 years, using 3-yr averages at start and end |
| 6 | Moderate P/E | Price ≤ **15×** average earnings of past 3 years |
| 7 | Moderate P/B | Price ≤ **1.5×** book value; or **P/E × P/B ≤ 22.5** (e.g., 9× earnings and 2.5× book qualifies) |

- These criteria exclude most stocks in two ways: weak/small/erratic companies, and expensive "quality" companies.
- Derived Graham Number: $\sqrt{22.5 \times \text{EPS} \times \text{BVPS}}$ (max price that passes test 7 with EPS on a 3-yr avg basis).
- Zweig (2003): few stocks pass today; that is itself a valuation signal. A defensive investor can simply index.

## 6. Enterprising Investor (Ch. 6, 7, 15)

### Don'ts (Ch. 6)
- Avoid second-grade bonds and preferreds unless bought at deep discounts (≥ ~30% below par) and the enterprising investor truly knows what they're doing.
- Avoid foreign government bonds (for the 1970s reader) and new issues/IPOs. Zweig: IPO = "It's Probably Overpriced"; first-day pops are mostly speculation.
- Avoid stocks of companies with recent spectacular earnings that the market is excited about.
- Zweig: day trading, chasing momentum, and acting on online tips are speculation; costs and taxes destroy returns.

### Do's (Ch. 7): four areas
1. **Relatively unpopular large companies:** low P/E among big companies (e.g., the lowest-P/E Dow stocks beat the high-P/E ones in most periods 1937–69). Large size protects: resources to recover, and the market eventually re-rates them.
2. **Bargain issues:** value ≥ 50% above price. Find via earnings power (normal earnings × conservative multiple) or assets. Best case: price below **net current assets** after deducting all prior claims, counting fixed assets as zero.
   - 1957 study: 85 net-current-asset stocks gained ~75% in two years vs ~50% for S&P industrials; almost no significant losses.
3. **Secondary companies (not industry leaders):** often undervalued. Buy only at **≤ 2/3 of appraised value**. Gains come from dividends, reinvested earnings, bull markets, and re-rating.
4. **Special situations ("workouts"):** mergers, liquidations, reorganizations, arbitrage. Specialist territory.

### Enterprising Screen (Ch. 15) [verified]
Start with low multipliers (P/E < ~10), then require:

| # | Criterion | Threshold |
|---|-----------|-----------|
| 1 | Financial condition | Current ratio ≥ **1.5**; debt ≤ **110%** of net current assets (industrials) |
| 2 | Earnings stability | No deficit in last **5 years** |
| 3 | Dividend record | Some current dividend |
| 4 | Earnings growth | Last year's earnings > those of ~5 years ago |
| 5 | Price | < **120%** of net tangible assets |

- Net-current-asset stocks ("net-nets"): buy a **diversified group** (dozens) below NCAV; individual ones can fail, but the group works.
- Zweig: low-priced stocks (< ~$1) have high trading costs, delisting risk, and a tendency to go out of business. They're OK only in a diversified basket.

## 7. Security Analysis for the Lay Investor (Ch. 11–13)

### Bond / Preferred safety: minimum earnings coverage of fixed charges (Table 11-1) [verified]
| Enterprise | Pretax, 7-yr avg | Pretax, poorest year | After-tax, 7-yr avg | After-tax, poorest year |
|------------|------------------|----------------------|---------------------|-------------------------|
| Public utility | 4× | 3× | 2.65× | 2.10× |
| Railroad | 5× | 4× | 3.20× | 2.65× |
| Industrial | 7× | 5× | 4.30× | 3.20× |
| Retail | 5× | 4× | 3.20× | 2.65× |

- Preferreds: same coverage, but on fixed charges + 2× preferred dividends.
- Alternative for high-rate eras: pretax earnings as % of debt principal ≥ 33% industrial, 20% utility, 25% railroad.
- Other tests: size of enterprise; stock/equity ratio (market value of stock vs debt); property value.

### Factors in a stock's capitalization rate (P/E)
1. General long-term prospects
2. Management
3. Financial strength and capital structure
4. Dividend record
5. Current dividend rate

### Growth-stock valuation formula [verified]
$$V = E_{normal} \times (8.5 + 2g)$$
- 8.5 = P/E for zero growth; g = expected annual growth over the next **7–10 years**.
- Can be reversed to find the growth rate the market price implies (e.g., Xerox implied ~32% growth vs GM 2.8%).
- Graham warns: growth projections are unreliable, and the higher the growth assumed, the more speculative the value. Zweig's commentary adds that the formula is not a precise valuation tool. Use only as a sanity check.

### Per-share earnings (Ch. 12)
- Use **average earnings over 7–10 years** rather than one year's figure.
- Watch special charges, write-offs taken in bad years to flatter later years, tax-loss carryforwards, dilution from convertibles/warrants/options (use fully diluted EPS), depreciation/inventory (LIFO/FIFO) method changes.
- Zweig red flags: "pro forma" earnings, capitalized operating costs, receivables growing faster than sales, recurring "nonrecurring" charges, aggressive pension-return assumptions, earnings from acquisitions, poor footnote disclosure.

### Four-company comparison (Ch. 13: ELTRA, Emerson Electric, Emery Air Freight, Emhart)
- High-multiple glamour stocks (Emerson, Emery) priced growth far into the future and carried speculative risk; lower-multiple ELTRA and Emhart offered more value per dollar and better margin of safety.
- Method: compare price, P/E, P/B, dividend yield, sales, net margin, ROE (earnings on book), 10-yr growth, earnings stability, financial strength, side by side.

## 8. Funds & Advisers (Ch. 9–10)

- Funds as a group can't beat the market they make up; "performance funds" that chase hot stocks crash (Manhattan Fund: strong 1967, then large losses).
- Closed-end funds at a discount to NAV are often better buys than open-end funds sold at a premium/load.
- Zweig fund rules: prefer index funds; choose managers with low turnover, owning their own fund, closed to new investors when too big, low expenses. Max annual expense ratios: bond funds 0.75%, US large-cap stock 1.0%, high-yield bonds 1.0%, small-cap 1.25%, international 1.5%.
- Past outperformance is mostly not persistent; high costs are reliably persistent.
- Advisers: choose for integrity and competence; they shouldn't promise outsized returns. Beware brokers whose pay depends on your trading.

## 9. Convertibles, Warrants (Ch. 16)

- Convertibles are usually less attractive than they look: the issuer gains from the conversion feature, and investors often end up with a weaker bond and a limited upside.
- Warrants dilute common shareholders and create a false impression of value; Graham regards their mass issuance as a "near fraud" on shareholders.

## 10. Case Histories & Comparisons (Ch. 17–18)

- **Penn Central:** weak interest coverage and dubious accounting were visible years before bankruptcy. Investors who applied basic bond-coverage tests would have avoided it.
- **Ling-Temco-Vought:** empire built on debt-financed acquisitions and accounting tricks; collapsed.
- **NVF / Sharon Steel:** a small company took over a much larger one via debt and warrants. Lesson: leverage and paper-financed takeovers create fragile, overpriced structures.
- **AAA Enterprises:** hot IPO of a trivial business at a huge multiple; went bankrupt.
- **Eight-pair comparisons (Ch. 18):** similar companies often sell at wildly different multiples. The market overpays for glamour and promotion, underpays for dull, solid businesses. Value per dollar matters more than the company's fame.

## 11. Shareholders & Management (Ch. 19)

- Shareholders should judge management by results and demand action (or sale) when results are poor relative to similar companies.
- Dividend policy: retained earnings must be justified by productive reinvestment. Zweig: insist on buybacks only when stock is cheap, watch for buybacks that just offset option dilution, excessive pay, and managers who ignore owners.

## 12. Margin of Safety: The Central Concept (Ch. 20)

- Margin of safety turns risk of error into a manageable factor; the purpose is to make an accurate forecast of the future unnecessary.
- **Bonds:** earning power well above fixed charges over many years.
- **Typical stocks:** earning power (earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E) well above the bond rate. Over 10 years the excess may aggregate ~50% of the price paid. With such a margin in each of a diversified list of **20+ stocks**, a favorable result is very likely.
- **Bargains:** price well below appraised value.
- **Growth stocks:** margin depends on growth estimates being conservative; at high prices there's none.
- Diversification is the companion of margin of safety: a margin makes profit more likely than loss for each holding, and diversification makes the aggregate outcome dependable.
- "Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike."

| Rule | Threshold | Ch. |
|------|-----------|-----|
| Stock allocation | 25%–75%, default 50% | 4 |
| Rebalance trigger | ~5-pt drift (or every 6 months, Zweig) | 4 |
| Mad money | ≤ 10% (Zweig) | 1 |
| Defensive # of stocks | 10–30 | 5 |
| Defensive P/E cap | ≤ 25× 7-yr avg EPS and ≤ 20× TTM | 5 |
| Ch. 14 current ratio | ≥ 2.0 | 14 |
| Ch. 14 LT debt | ≤ net current assets | 14 |
| Ch. 14 earnings stability | 10 yrs positive | 14 |
| Ch. 14 dividends | 20 yrs uninterrupted | 14 |
| Ch. 14 growth | ≥ 33% over 10 yrs (3-yr avgs) | 14 |
| Ch. 14 P/E | ≤ 15× 3-yr avg EPS | 14 |
| Ch. 14 P/B | ≤ 1.5, or P/E × P/B ≤ 22.5 | 14 |
| Price vs tangible book (conservative) | ≤ ~1.33× | 8 |
| Bargain issue | value ≥ 150% of price | 7 |
| Secondary company | price ≤ 2/3 appraised value | 7 |
| Ch. 15 current ratio | ≥ 1.5 | 15 |
| Ch. 15 debt | ≤ 110% of net current assets | 15 |
| Ch. 15 earnings | no deficit 5 yrs, growth vs ~5 yrs ago | 15 |
| Ch. 15 price | < 120% net tangible assets | 15 |
| Net-net | price < NCAV, diversified basket | 15 |
| Bond coverage (industrial) | 7× pretax 7-yr avg / 5× poorest | 11 |
| Growth formula | V = E × (8.5 + 2g) | 11 |
| Shiller P/E danger | > ~20 (Zweig) | 3 |

## 14. Red Flags

- No thorough analysis, or a "story" in place of numbers
- High P/E on a single year's peak earnings; growth extrapolated far into the future
- Weak current ratio, debt exceeding working capital, thin interest coverage
- Deficits in recent years; erratic or skipped dividends
- Acquisition-driven growth, heavy use of stock/warrants as currency
- Accounting changes, big one-time write-offs, "pro forma" numbers, receivables or inventories growing faster than sales
- Hot IPOs, new-issue booms, high fund turnover and fees
- Your own excitement, fear, or urge to act on recent price moves

## 15. Quotes

- "The investor's chief problem—and even his worst enemy—is likely to be himself." (Ch. 8)
- "Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike." (Ch. 20)
- The three-word motto of sound investment: **"Margin of Safety."** (Ch. 20)
- Mr. Market's quotations are there to be taken advantage of, not to be followed. (Ch. 8, paraphrase)
